title: Marcus Aurelius and His Son Commodus
text:
For most of the second century, Roman emperors chose their successors by adoption, picking capable adult men. Marcus Aurelius had himself been adopted in this way, and trained for years before taking power in 161. He was a philosopher on the throne, whose private notebook, the Meditations, is still read today. But unlike his predecessors, he had a surviving son of his own: Commodus, born in 161.

Marcus gave the boy the best teachers available and raised him to rule. In 177, when Commodus was fifteen, his father made him co-emperor. Commodus accompanied Marcus on his long campaigns against the Germanic tribes along the Danube. In March 180 Marcus died in his camp, and Commodus, now eighteen, became sole emperor.

He quickly made peace with the tribes and returned to the pleasures of Rome. The historian Cassius Dio, who was a senator at the time, wrote that Commodus was not naturally wicked but simple and easily led by bad companions. His reign turned into a series of plots and executions. He handed government to favorites, renamed Rome after himself and fought as a gladiator in the arena before the horrified senate. On the last day of 192 he was strangled by a wrestler on the orders of his own household.

Dio wrote that with the death of Marcus, Roman history descended from a kingdom of gold to one of iron and rust.
lesson: Even the wisest parent cannot guarantee a child's character, and love can blind us to a child's unfitness. Handing someone power is different from preparing them for it.
source: Cassius Dio, Roman History 72 (71).34 to 73 (72).22; Historia Augusta, Life of Commodus
